props.title: The 400 Blows
props.initialSlug: A rebellious teen's descent into delinquency in Paris

sections.content: The 400 Blows (1959) launched the French New Wave with raw emotional power, following young Antoine Doinel through the streets of Paris. François Truffaut's semi-autobiographical debut feature ripped apart polite cinema conventions - handheld cameras follow Antoine's restless energy, jump cuts compress time jarringly, and that final freeze-frame of Antoine staring at the ocean became one of cinema's most iconic endings. The film's DNA shows up in later youth rebellion classics like If.... (1968) and Dead Poets Society (1989), but none match its intimate portrait of adolescent alienation.

sections.content: Truffaut's raw approach influenced a generation of filmmakers tackling youth alienation. Rebel Without a Cause (1955) preceded it but feels theatrical in comparison. Later films like The Graduate (1967) and Harold and Maude (1971) echo Antoine's existential malaise, while modern coming-of-age stories like Boyhood (2014) and Lady Bird (2017) still draw from its well of authentic adolescent experience. The film's technical innovations - location shooting, natural lighting, long tracking shots - became hallmarks of the French New Wave.

Beyond its technical achievements, The 400 Blows captures the universal experience of feeling misunderstood. Antoine's troubled relationship with authority - parents, teachers, police - resonates across cultures and decades. Later French films like La Haine (1995) and Water Lilies (2007) inherit its unflinching look at youth on society's margins. Even American indies like Kids (1995) and The Florida Project (2017) share its documentary-like attention to childhood's raw edges. SUBHEAD: Impact on Global Cinema

movies.title: Zero for Conduct
movies.slug: Jean Vigo's rebellious boarding school film directly influenced The 400 Blows with its anarchic spirit

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond France. Japanese master Yasujirō Ozu praised its intimate family dynamics, while Italian Neorealists recognized their own style in its street-level authenticity. Bicycle Thieves (1948) shares its humanitarian perspective, while later works like Truffaut's own Small Change (1976) and Abbas Kiarostami's Where Is the Friend's House? (1987) continue its tradition of seeing the world through children's eyes with respect and complexity.
